newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel pledges Bonn to strive to enter EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel pledges Bonn to strive to enter EMU.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel pledged on Tuesday to redouble Bonn's efforts aimed at readying Germany to join Europe's planned currency union with the first wave of nations at the end of the decade.

"We will take all possible steps to ensure that Germany will meet the convergence criteria now and always," Waigel told an international audience during Global 24, a video conference on European monetary union.
Europe's currency union is scheduled to begin on January 1, 1999, with countries meeting a variety of entry qualifications on deficits, debt, inflation and interest rates for example.
Waigel spoke at a particularly sensitive time as many European states, including the once model student Germany, struggle to meet the entry criteria.

Over the past weeks the Bonn finance ministry has announced plans to press on with privatisations and sell more of its stake in telecommunications group Deutsche Telekom all to raise money to help paper over a gaping deficit.
At the same time, even as senior officials routinely say France and Germany would both join the union, Waigel warned that no country had been granted automatic entry into the currency union.
"There is no automatic entry for any country and no one will be arbitrarily excluded either," Waigel told the conference.
Waigel pointedly refused to speculate which EU states might next spring be allowed to enter the currency union.
Government officials will assess each country's 1997 economic data next spring to determine the circle of nations which will launch the currency union.
Separately German Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Munich adopted language usually used by Germany's ultra conservative politicians and insisted that Germany would meet a deficit criterion of 3.0 percent.
Kohl like the Bundesbank has traditionally avoided discussions involving precise levels, preferring to speak more generally about the Maastricht Treaty and that the criteria must be met strictly.

Sources close to the Bundesbank said that Kohl's shift in language and Waigel's statements could be interpreted as a thinly veiled suggestion that France needs to work harder to meet Maastricht Treaty entry criteria.
France recently said it would exceed the 3.0 percent deficit target this year, signalling the deficit would be quite a bit higher.
For Germany however such an overshooting would be wholly unacceptable, sources close to the Bundesbank said.
